reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Python Fundamentals & Business Context
slides.transcript:
Welcome to IAN 601, Introduction to Data Analytics Methods and Approaches. This course is designed to build your data analytics skills step by step, starting with Python fundamentals and gradually moving into practical data analysis.

Across the fourteen modules, we begin with variables, decisions, functions, and core data structures. Then we move into organizing larger Python programs, more advanced Python techniques, professional coding practices, NumPy, and Pandas. In the later modules, we focus on advanced Pandas, data cleaning and exploratory analysis, statistics and visualization, and finally an introduction to machine learning and working with external data.

[tts-break]

Module 1 is where that foundation begins. We’ll learn how Python stores values, understands data types, performs calculations, and presents results clearly. You do not need to memorize every symbol. Focus on the logic. In analytics, we usually start with data, apply a rule or calculation, and produce a result that helps us answer a question.

As we go, keep connecting the code to something real. A value might represent sales, cost, age, temperature, or another measurement. By the end of the module, you’ll combine these ideas in a small sales calculator and be able to explain what each line is doing.

slides.title: How to use this slide lesson
slides.transcript:
Use these slides actively. Read the idea first, pause for a moment, and predict what you think the code will do before you run it.

After you run an example, change one value and run it again. Small changes are one of the best ways to understand Python because you can immediately see which part of the output depends on which input.

[tts-break]

For example, if sales is one thousand dollars, run the calculation once. Then change sales to twelve hundred fifty and see what changes. Ask yourself why the result moved.

The editor looks like VS Code, but the Python ideas are the same whether you use VS Code, Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab, or another environment.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 1
slides.transcript:
Here is the path we’ll follow. We begin with variables, because variables give names to values. Then we look at data types so Python can distinguish numbers, text, and True or False values.

Next, we use arithmetic to create useful metrics, then we format results so they are easier for people to read. We also look at type conversion because data often arrives as text even when we eventually want to calculate with it.

[tts-break]

Everything builds toward a small sales calculator. If you can follow how a value moves from raw input to calculation and finally to readable output, you have the main idea of this module.

slides.title: What is Python doing for us?
slides.transcript:
Before writing more code, think about what Python is doing for us as analysts. Python lets us describe a repeatable process once and then reuse it whenever new data arrives.

A simple analytics workflow often looks like this: represent information with variables, transform those values with calculations, and communicate the result with readable output.

[tts-break]

Suppose we begin with sales and costs. Those are raw values. We subtract costs from sales to create profit. Profit is a derived metric because we created it from other values. Then we display the result so another person can understand it.

That pattern—raw value, code, derived metric, readable result—comes up again and again in analytics.

slides.title: Variables store values
slides.transcript:
Let’s start with variables. A variable is simply a meaningful name connected to a value.

If a company has one thousand dollars in sales, we can store that value in a variable named sales. We can do the same with costs. Once those values have names, a formula such as sales minus costs is much easier to understand than a formula made only of numbers.

[tts-break]

Good variable names communicate meaning. Names like monthly_sales, patient_age, or total_cost tell the reader what the data represents. A vague name like x may work, but it makes the code harder to read.

Variables also make code reusable. Change the value, and the same calculation can run again.

slides.title: Code: store values in variables
slides.transcript:
Let’s run our first complete example with variables.

Sales is one thousand, costs is eight hundred, and profit is calculated by subtracting costs from sales. So before you run the cell, you should already expect profit to be two hundred.

The print statements simply make those three values visible in the output.

[tts-break]

Now change sales from one thousand to twelve hundred fifty and run the cell again. Notice that you do not need to rewrite the profit formula. Python automatically uses the new value of sales.

That is a basic but important idea in analytics: the logic can stay the same even when the data changes.

slides.title: Visual: variables become metrics
slides.transcript:
Now connect the code to the visual. Sales is one thousand dollars, costs are eight hundred dollars, and profit becomes two hundred dollars.

The key idea is that profit was not directly entered. We created it from the other values. That makes it a derived metric.

[tts-break]

Many familiar measures work the same way. Profit margin, growth rate, average order value, and conversion rate are all built from other values.

If you change sales or costs, the profit bar should move too. That visual connection helps reinforce how inputs drive derived metrics.

slides.title: Variables can be reassigned
slides.transcript:
A variable does not have to keep the same value forever. Python lets us assign a new value to an existing variable.

At first, sales is one thousand. After the second assignment, sales becomes fifteen hundred. When Python reaches the second print statement, it uses the most recent value.

[tts-break]

This is called reassignment. It is common when information changes during a workflow—for example, replacing an estimate with an updated value.

Use reassignment carefully. The value may change, but the variable name should still describe the same kind of information.

slides.title: Assign several values at once
slides.transcript:
Python can assign several values in one line. Here, Jordan goes into employee_name, thirty goes into age, and fifty thousand goes into salary.

The order matters. The first value is matched with the first variable, the second with the second, and so on.

[tts-break]

This feature is convenient when the values clearly belong together, but readability still matters. If one line becomes crowded or confusing, separate assignments are perfectly fine.

Run the example, then replace the fictional values with another set and confirm that each variable receives the correct value.

slides.title: Variable naming rules and habits
slides.transcript:
Good variable names make code easier to understand. Monthly_sales is descriptive, and patient_age is clear because the words are separated with an underscore.

Short names such as ms might save a few keystrokes, but they force the reader to guess what the variable means.

[tts-break]

There are also syntax rules. A variable name cannot begin with a number, and it cannot contain spaces. Python programmers commonly use lowercase words separated by underscores.

A useful test is to imagine opening your code again six months from now. If the names still make sense without extra explanation, they are probably good names.

slides.title: Data types tell Python what values mean
slides.transcript:
Now we move from variable names to data types. A data type tells Python what kind of value it is working with and what operations make sense.

An integer is a whole number. A float includes a decimal. A string represents text. A Boolean stores True or False.

[tts-break]

The meaning matters. Twelve visits is naturally an integer because it is a count. Nineteen point ninety-nine is a float when it represents a price. A city name is text, and an active flag is Boolean.

Before calculating with any value, think about what it represents—not just what it looks like.

slides.title: Code: inspect data types
slides.transcript:
Let’s inspect a few values with Python’s type function.

Age is thirty, so Python sees an integer. Height is five point nine, so that is a float. Jordan is text, so the type is string. True is a Boolean.

Run the cell and verify those four results.

[tts-break]

Then put quotation marks around thirty. To us it still looks like the number thirty, but Python now sees text. That small change can affect whether arithmetic works correctly.

Checking types is one of the simplest ways to diagnose confusing behavior in a data workflow.

slides.title: Some numbers should stay as text
slides.transcript:
Not every value made of digits should be numeric. Some values are identifiers rather than quantities.

Take employee ID zero zero one two five. We do not add or average employee IDs. We use them to identify records. If we store that ID as a number, the leading zeros disappear.

[tts-break]

The same issue appears with ZIP codes, account numbers, product codes, and many other identifiers.

A better question than “Does this value contain digits?” is “Do I plan to calculate with this value?” If not, and the exact formatting matters, text is often the right choice.

slides.title: Arithmetic creates derived metrics
slides.transcript:
Arithmetic lets us turn raw values into useful metrics.

Sales minus costs gives profit. Profit divided by sales can give a margin. Profit minus tax can give net profit. These are derived metrics because they are created from other values.

[tts-break]

Python uses familiar operators: plus for addition, minus for subtraction, an asterisk for multiplication, a forward slash for division, and two asterisks for exponentiation.

The formula matters more than the syntax. Python can run a perfectly valid calculation that represents the wrong business idea, so always understand the meaning of the metric before trusting the result.

slides.title: Code: calculate profit and tax
slides.transcript:
Let’s trace this calculation carefully.

Sales is one thousand and costs are eight hundred, so profit is two hundred. Tax is five percent of profit. Five percent is zero point zero five, so the tax becomes ten dollars. Net profit is two hundred minus ten, which gives one hundred ninety dollars.

[tts-break]

Notice the dependency chain. Net profit depends on tax. Tax depends on profit. Profit depends on sales and costs.

That kind of chain is common in analytics. Change the tax rate to ten percent, predict the new result, and then run the cell to check yourself.

slides.title: Three useful operators
slides.transcript:
Here are three operators that are easy to overlook but very useful.

Two asterisks mean exponentiation, so two to the power of three equals eight. Double forward slashes give whole-number division. One hundred twenty-five floor-divided by sixty gives two complete groups of sixty.

The percent sign gives the remainder, so one hundred twenty-five modulo sixty gives five.

[tts-break]

Floor division and modulo often work together. For one hundred twenty-five minutes, floor division tells us there are two full hours and modulo tells us five minutes remain.

Run the example and make sure the logic makes sense, not just the output.

slides.title: Parentheses control calculation order
slides.transcript:
Calculation order matters. Python follows the normal rules of arithmetic, so multiplication happens before addition unless parentheses change the grouping.

Ten plus five times two becomes twenty because five times two happens first. But when we write parentheses around ten plus five, Python calculates fifteen first, then multiplies by two to get thirty.

[tts-break]

Both expressions are valid. Neither produces an error. The danger is that a wrong formula can still run successfully.

Use parentheses when they make the intended calculation clearer for you and for anyone else reading the code.

slides.title: Print makes results visible
slides.transcript:
The print function gives us a quick way to see what the program is doing.

Here we store a name, age, sales, and costs. The print statements combine labels with values so the output has context.

The last line calculates sales minus costs directly, so with one thousand in sales and eight hundred in costs, the displayed profit is two hundred.

[tts-break]

Print is simple, but it is extremely useful while learning and debugging. If you are unsure what a variable contains at a certain point, printing it is often the fastest way to inspect the program state.

slides.title: f-strings create readable messages
slides.transcript:
Now we make output cleaner with f-strings.

An f-string begins with the letter f before the quotation mark. Curly braces mark the places where Python should insert variable values or expressions.

Patient A and age forty-five are inserted directly into the text. For temperature, colon dot one f tells Python to display one digit after the decimal point.

[tts-break]

So ninety-eight point six three four five becomes ninety-eight point six in the output.

The important idea is that good analytical output includes both the value and enough context for another person to understand it.

slides.title: Format money and percentages
slides.transcript:
Formatting changes how a number is displayed, not the numeric value itself.

For revenue, comma dot two f adds thousands separators and keeps two digits after the decimal point. That makes large monetary values much easier to read.

For growth, percent formatting turns zero point one five six seven eight into fifteen point six eight percent.

[tts-break]

Different outputs call for different formats. Money usually needs commas and decimals. Rates often make more sense as percentages. Scientific notation is useful for very large or very small numbers.

Good formatting helps the reader interpret the result quickly.

slides.title: Input usually starts as text
slides.transcript:
A common source of confusion is that data often arrives as text. Forms, CSV files, APIs, and user input frequently give us strings even when the characters look numeric.

The text “29.99” looks like a price to us, but Python may still treat it as a string.

[tts-break]

Before doing arithmetic, we convert the text to an appropriate numeric type. Float is useful for decimal values, while int is useful for whole numbers.

The pattern is simple: receive text, convert it, then calculate.

slides.title: Code: convert text into numbers
slides.transcript:
Let’s apply that conversion pattern.

Price begins as the text “29.99” and quantity begins as the text “5”. Float converts the price to a decimal number. Int converts the quantity to a whole number.

Now Python can multiply them. Twenty-nine dollars and ninety-nine cents times five gives one hundred forty-nine dollars and ninety-five cents.

[tts-break]

The final f-string formats that number as money.

Change the quantity from five to eight, predict the new total, and then run the code. This is a very typical data-cleaning step.

slides.title: Boolean conversion previews decision logic
slides.transcript:
Boolean values represent True and False. They become especially important when we start writing conditions and filters.

Zero converts to False. A nonzero number such as one becomes True. An empty string becomes False, while nonempty text such as “Hello” becomes True.

[tts-break]

This gives us a preview of the logic used in the next module. Programs often ask questions such as: does a value exist, is an amount above a threshold, or does a record meet a rule?

Those questions eventually evaluate to True or False.

slides.title: Preview a conversion error
slides.transcript:
Now consider what happens when the text cannot be converted to a number.

The variable contains “abc”. Calling float on that text would fail because those characters do not represent a numeric value.

The example performs a simple check first. It removes one decimal point if there is one, then uses isdigit to see whether the remaining characters are digits.

[tts-break]

With “abc”, the condition is false, so the program prints a warning instead of attempting the conversion.

This is only a simple preview of validation. Real data can contain negative signs, spaces, commas, missing values, and other complications. The key idea is to check assumptions before trusting incoming data.

slides.title: Practice: small tasks
slides.transcript:
Now it is time to combine the ideas in short exercises.

Start by creating variables for a fictional patient and printing them. Then inspect types for an identifier, an amount, and a Boolean flag. After that, calculate something simple such as area and perimeter.

[tts-break]

Move next to a revenue statement with formatted money, and then calculate profit and margin from sales and costs.

Do not rush through the tasks. For each one, explain what the variables represent, why their types make sense, and what the output means.

slides.title: Practice code: patient variables
slides.transcript:
This practice example represents one fictional patient record with four different data types.

Patient_label is text, age is an integer, temperature is a float, and is_follow_up is Boolean. The f-strings turn those values into readable output.

[tts-break]

Run the example once, then change the values. As you edit, ask why each type makes sense. You would not average a patient label, but averaging temperatures could be meaningful because temperature is numeric.

Thinking about meaning and type together is an important data habit.

slides.title: Practice code: profit and margin
slides.transcript:
Here we combine variables, arithmetic, and formatting in one example.

Sales are twenty-five hundred dollars and costs are seventeen hundred fifty dollars, so profit is seven hundred fifty dollars. Margin is profit divided by sales, which gives zero point three, or thirty percent when formatted.

[tts-break]

Profit and margin describe related but different ideas. Profit is a dollar amount. Margin is a ratio that tells us what share of sales remains as profit.

Increase costs and run the example again. Both profit and margin should move downward.

slides.title: Mini project: simple sales calculator
slides.transcript:
This mini project brings the whole module together.

Sales are forty-two hundred dollars, costs are thirty-one hundred dollars, and the tax rate is six percent. Profit is eleven hundred. Tax is sixty-six. Net profit becomes one thousand thirty-four dollars.

Then net profit is divided by sales to get a net margin of about twenty-four point six percent.

[tts-break]

Notice how many Module 1 ideas appear here: meaningful variables, numeric types, arithmetic, derived metrics, f-strings, money formatting, and percentages.

Change one input, predict which outputs should move, and then run the code to verify your reasoning.

slides.title: Self-check
slides.transcript:
Use these questions as a quick check before finishing the module.

Can you explain what a variable is? Can you tell the difference between an integer, float, string, and Boolean? Can you trace a calculation from input values to a final result?

[tts-break]

Also think about formatting and conversion. Why would we display a decimal as a percentage? Why might the text “29.99” need conversion before arithmetic?

You do not need to memorize every symbol yet. What matters is understanding the concepts well enough to recognize what Python needs.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let’s bring the main ideas together.

Variables give names to values. Data types tell Python what those values mean. Arithmetic creates derived metrics. Formatting helps us communicate results clearly. Type conversion helps when data arrives in the wrong form for calculation.

[tts-break]

The larger pattern is simple: store the data, understand its type, transform it, and communicate the result.

Next, we add decisions and repetition with if statements, for loops, and while loops.

[tts-break]

In Module 2, we’ll build directly on this foundation by giving Python the ability to make decisions and repeat work. You’ll use conditions, if statements, for loops, and while loops to classify values, apply rules, and process more than one observation at a time. That is where your programs begin to behave more like real analytical workflows.
